title: Baladeva Vidyabhushana
html:
The Gaudiya Vedanta-acharya

Srila Baladeva Vidyabhushana lived in the eighteenth century; a younger contemporary and shiksha-disciple of Vishvanatha Chakravarti Thakura, he holds a place of his own in the history of the Gaudiya Vaishnavas: he was the first acharya of the line to write a commentary on the “Vedanta-sutra,” and for this he is called the Gaudiya Vedanta-acharya. The biographies name him Sri Baladeva, Baladeva Prabhu, Shrimad Baladeva Vidyabhushana Prabhu and Shripada Baladeva Vidyabhushana, while in the colophons of his books he signs himself simply “Vidyabhushana.” Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati, quoting his explanations in the “Anubhashya,” calls him Srila and Shripada Baladeva Vidyabhushana.

He had another name as well, Govinda Dasa, “the servant of Govinda”: he was so called for his service to Govinda, the Deity of Sri Rupa. According to one of the biographies, he received the name “Ekanti Govinda Dasa” when he accepted the dress of a Vaishnava vairagi.1 The title “Vidyabhushana,” “adorned with learning,” is connected with his chief work, the “Govinda-bhashya,” of which more will be said below.

In the sampradaya he is called “the avatara of Jiva Gosvami.” This is not an identification from the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” but a saying of the devotees, and its meaning lies elsewhere: Baladeva may be called a second Jiva. Both were philosophers, superb grammarians and poets, and both wrote with originality; Jiva created the philosophical shastras of the sampradaya, and Baladeva showed that teaching in all the principal scriptures, inheriting from Jiva a keen mind for refuting opponents. One of the biographies speaks of him as a devotee of the purest and loftiest kind, whose only concern was to serve the Lord, untouched by any wish for name or fame, and who composed a wealth of jewel-like shastras for the highest good of all who are born human.

A Son of Orissa

Little is known of his family. It is said that he was born in a village near Remuna, in the Baleshvara (Balasore) district of Orissa. Some biographies call his family Khandaits, others Vaishya farmers; his parents' names have not been preserved, and nothing is known of how he was born or how he spent his early years.2 Nor is it known when he was born. He nowhere says so himself, and the biographies judge by indirect signs: one, reasoning that at the time of the dispute in Galta (1704) he cannot have been less than twenty, considers that he was probably born in the 1680s, “until reliable sources are found”; others place his birth in the seventeenth century or at the beginning of the eighteenth.3 His appearance day is not in the calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math either.

His homeland itself, however, explains a great deal. At the end of the sixteenth century and the beginning of the seventeenth, the Balasore district was transformed by the preaching of Shyamananda and Rasikananda Murari, carried on by Rasikananda's son Radhananda, his grandson Nayanananda and their followers. Baladeva's early attraction to the teaching of Sri Chaitanya undoubtedly grew from this soil.

Study and the School of Madhva

While still young he studied Sanskrit grammar, poetry, poetics and logic and became an expert in them. According to one of the biographies, he studied in a village by Lake Chilka in the south of Orissa; there he took up Vedanta, and to understand its commentaries more deeply he went to Mysore. There he was especially struck by the coherence and logical consistency of Madhvacharya's commentary on the “Vedanta-sutra”; he became a student of that school and lived in a monastery of the Tattvavadis. Another biography names no place: having finished his studies, he went on pilgrimage and stayed at a Tattvavadi temple, the followers of Madhva, where he thoroughly mastered their siddhanta.4

In that school he accepted sannyasa. He preached Tattvavada with great force throughout India and, travelling, came to Purushottama-kshetra, Jagannatha Puri. There he debated with the local scholars, showing the depth of his learning, and his fame quickly spread through the region.

The books of our line also speak of his Madhva past. “Our Teachers” says that before accepting Mahaprabhu's teaching he belonged to the Madhva-sampradaya, and therefore knew equally well both the teaching of the Gaudiyas and the doctrine of Madhvacharya. Srila B. R. Sridhar Maharaj says of him: “Baladeva Vidyabhusana was very akin to the Madhva sampradaya,” and even: “He may be a member of another line, the Madhva sampradaya, in the physical sense” (“Sri Guru and His Grace”). This path was not a change of faith in any worldly sense: a line close to Mahaprabhu led a seeker of truth to the fullness of His teaching.5

Radha-Damodara

In Puri he met the pandit Sri Radha-Damodara and spoke with him about the principles of bhakti. Radha-Damodara told him of Gaurasundara's merciful pastimes and of how the Lord revealed the Gaudiya Vaishnava siddhanta to Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya. These accounts deeply moved Baladeva's heart. For some days he listened, and then Radha-Damodara initiated him in the mantra of Radha and Krishna and began to study Sri Jiva's “Shat-sandarbha” at his feet. So one of the biographies tells it; another adds that Radha-Damodara was a scholar from Kanauj and that Baladeva accepted initiation only after he had studied the “Shat-sandarbha” and become convinced of the superiority of Gaudiya Vaishnava philosophy. According to a third biography, Radha-Damodara was at that time the head of the Shyamasundara-kunja math in Vrindavana, founded by Shyamananda.6

Radha-Damodara belonged to the line of Shyamananda, a branch of the succession of Nityananda Prabhu. According to one of the biographies, the chain of disciples is: Gauri Dasa Pandita — Hridaya Chaitanya — Shyamananda — Rasikananda — Nayanananda — Radha-Damodara — Baladeva; Baladeva's parama-guru is thus Nayanananda, the grandson of Rasikananda. According to another, Radha-Damodara was a disciple of Rasikananda himself. A certain Krishna Dasa was Baladeva's fellow student; the biography does not say who he was.7

At the Feet of Vishvanatha

Baladeva studied under three teachers. He learned Vedanta from Radha-Damodara, the “Bhagavata” from Vishvanatha Chakravarti and the other shastras from Pitambara. All three were profound knowers of the scriptures and souls of the highest spiritual standing. As Jiva had once been taught by his elders, Rupa and Sanatana, so Baladeva was taught by Vishvanatha and his other teachers; and Baladeva's very interests and range of learning matched Jiva's exactly.8

He remembers Pitambara with gratitude in the “Siddhanta-ratna” (8.35): by his mercy, Baladeva writes, he has gathered in this book the views of those who studied Vedanta — may it delight the learned. This Pitambara (Pitambara Dasa) is probably the author of the “Bhagavata-tattva-dipa-prakashavarana-bhanga,” a work of 2,910 shlokas, a manuscript of which, copied in 1796, is listed in Kielhorn's catalogue of manuscripts.9

When he had spent some time with Radha-Damodara, Baladeva went at his bidding to Vrindavana to deepen his knowledge of Gaudiya Vaishnavism at the feet of Vishvanatha Chakravarti; on the way he visited Navadvipa. Vishvanatha — Harivallabha Dasa — was delighted by the newcomer's submissiveness, humility, learning and renunciation; he kept him by his side for a time and taught him Sri Chaitanya's achintya-bhedabheda and the siddhanta of Gaudiya Krishna-bhakti. From then on his whole life was given to the teaching of the Gaudiya-sampradaya, and it alone was what he preached. Srila Sridhar Maharaj says the same: “when he came in connection with Visvanatha Chakravarti Thakur, he showed great interest in Gaudiya Vaishnavism” (“Sri Guru and His Grace”). Vishvanatha became his guru in the line of instruction, his shiksha-guru; diksha he received from Radha-Damodara.10

Baladeva lived as a renunciant: he accepted the dress of a Vaishnava vairagi, and one of the biographies calls him “an ideal sannyasi.”

The Dispute at Galta

To understand what the Gaudiyas owe Baladeva, one must recall what happened at the beginning of the eighteenth century in Galta, near Amber, the old capital of the Jaipur principality. When Sri Rupa's Govinda-deva was threatened by iconoclastic Muslims, a prince of Amber moved Him to Galta to keep Him safe. Yet Galta, since the time of Payohari Krishnadasa, the guru of Prithviraja (Man Singh's great-grandfather), had been the chief seat of the Ramanandis in northern India, and it was a prince of Amber who had given them land there. King Jai Singh built a huge temple in Galta and installed in it the Govinda-deva of Sri Rupa, whom the biography calls Man Singh's guru. The Ramanandis saw that the Gaudiyas were in even greater favour at the court of Amber than they were, and this galled them.11

As long as Man Singh and his descendants were close to the Gaudiya Vaishnava teachers, the Ramanandis did not dare to show hostility. But in time the firmness and learning of the Gaudiya priests of Govinda in Galta declined, their successors became mere temple servants, and then the local Ramanandi scholars and sadhus began to attack them in every way, to take from them the service of Govinda and drive the Gaudiyas out of Amber.

The Ramanandis' argument was this: the Gaudiyas have no right to serve as priests, because their sampradaya is not recognized. In support they cited a verse known from the “Padma-purana”:

“Mantras outside a sampradaya are considered fruitless. Therefore in Kali there will be four (founders of) sampradayas — the Vaishnavas Sri, Brahma, Rudra and Sanaka, who purify the earth.”12

A mantra bears no fruit until one joins one of the four sampradayas, whose acharyas are Ramanuja, Madhva, Vishnusvami and Nimbarka, and whose first gurus are Lakshmi, Brahma, Rudra and the Sanat-kumaras. The Ramanandis also demanded proof that Gaudiya philosophy was in harmony with Vedanta and the Upanishads. The Bengali priests could not defend themselves, and Jai Singh was greatly troubled.

King Jai Singh II, a man of deep learning, did not wish either to expel the Gaudiya priests or to hand over the Deity's service to the Ramanandis until the latter had debated with the leaders of the Gaudiyas themselves, and he invited Vishvanatha Chakravarti to Galta, to answer the opponents, establish the strength of the teaching and win recognition for the sampradaya. The challenge raised at the Jaipur court was simple: no acharya of the Gaudiyas had written a commentary on Vedanta. “Our Teachers” adds that the kings of Jaipur worshipped both Sri Sri Radha-Govinda and Lord Narayana, while the numerous Ramanandis opposed the worship of Radha-Govinda, held Narayana to be the principal Deity and claimed that Mahaprabhu's movement stood outside the four sampradayas, while Maharaja Jai Singh, a patron of the Gaudiyas who had studied the works of the Gosvamis, of Kaviraja Gosvami and of Vrindavana Dasa, arranged a debate on whose outcome the fate of worship in all Rajasthan depended.13

According to a tradition handed down in the line of teachers, the dispute in Galta took place in 1626 Shaka (1704); according to other accounts, around 1706 (1628 Shaka).14 Vishvanatha was by then too old for such a journey and sent his younger disciples in his place: Baladeva and his friend Krishnadeva Sarvabhauma, also a disciple of Vishvanatha; one of the biographies calls them “two rising stars of the Gaudiya Vaishnava world.” According to other accounts, Vishvanatha wanted one of the young scholarly devotees to represent the sampradaya; the choice fell on Baladeva, a master of all the principal shastras, and he went to Jaipur alone.15

Two Ways — and a Third

The question before the Gaudiyas was this. Either they belong to the sampradaya of Madhva — then let them prove their unity with it in philosophy and in the order of worship. Or they are independent — then they must have their own commentary on Vedanta: it was the established rule that a sampradaya claiming independence shows the foundation of its teaching in the Vedanta-sutras. The position of the Gaudiyas was unusual. Their historical roots lay in the line of Madhva, yet they did not regard his commentary on the sutras as their own, for they had accepted achintya-bhedabheda, whereas Madhva in his bhashya teaches difference;16 and in philosophy and in ritual they differed so much from the Madhvas that other sampradayas did not regard them as Madhvas.

Neither Sri Chaitanya nor the six Gosvamis accepted Madhva's bhashya in full as the teaching of the Gaudiyas, nor did they write a commentary of their own on the sutras. The Gosvamis quoted Madhva in support of their conclusions, but they also drew support from Ramanuja, Sridhara Svami and others. Sri Chaitanya, in Varanasi and on other occasions, affirmed that the true commentary on Vedanta is the “Bhagavata-purana”; Sanatana in the “Brihad-bhagavatamrita” and Jiva in the “Sandarbhas” strengthened this idea. But every Vaishnava reveres the “Bhagavata,” and it was not the exclusive property of the Gaudiyas; so the Ramanandis demanded one of two things: either prove identity with Madhva by accepting his bhashya and order of worship, or produce a commentary of their own.

Baladeva took another way. He showed that the Gaudiya-sampradaya descends in succession from the line of Madhva and that the foundations of its teaching and philosophy are found there, and at the same time he stressed what the Gaudiyas themselves had brought and how their teaching and practice differ. First he showed that both sampradayas agree in the nine truths taught by Madhva, and then how the Gaudiyas had unfolded them in their own way, up to achintya-bhedabheda. The Gaudiyas, then, are not cut off from Madhva: part of the edifice of their teaching stands on his doctrine of the difference between the jiva and Ishvara. But the edifice itself is Mahaprabhu's gift, and achintya-bhedabheda is not a concession to two contending schools or a midpoint between them, but the original conclusion of the shruti, revealed by Mahaprabhu and unfolded by the Gosvamis.17

Baladeva also pointed out that the idea of achintya-bhedabheda first appears in Madhva himself — in the “Bhagavata-tatparya” (11.7.51), where he quotes a verse of the ancient treatise “Brahma-tarka.” Sri Jiva knew that the seed of achintya-bhedabheda lay in the “Tatparya”: at the beginning of the “Shat-sandarbha” he says that he followed Madhva's “Tatparya” and accepted what it cites from the “Brahma-tarka,” though he had not found the treatise itself. Later Baladeva included this reasoning in the “Siddhanta-ratna,” the “Prameya-ratnavali,” the commentary on the “Govinda-bhashya” and other works of his, thereby paying deep respect to Madhva.

The Ramanandis were convinced that the Gaudiyas did indeed descend from Madhva and owed him something. But all the more insistently they demanded to see the Gaudiyas' own commentary: since they had something to say beyond Madhva and had a philosophical system of their own, let them show it in an exposition of the sutras. The “Bhagavata” they did not accept as a commentary on Vedanta. In this way they compelled Baladeva to compose the “Govinda-bhashya.”

Before a vast gathering of pandits Baladeva challenged all to a learned debate. The debate was long and heated, and no one could stand against his conclusions, learning and penetration. He maintained that Sri Chaitanya, from whom the Gaudiya-sampradaya comes, had accepted the “Srimad-Bhagavatam” as the best commentary on Vedanta, and that the Gaudiyas therefore did not feel they needed one of their own. So the “Charitamrita” teaches in Mahaprabhu's words:

“Therefore the Bhagavatam is the very meaning of the sutras: by nature it is the author's own commentary on the sutras he himself composed. ‘This book of eighteen thousand verses, named Srimad-Bhagavatam, is the meaning of the Brahma-sutras. It settles the sense of the Mahabharata, it is a commentary on the Gayatri, and it is enriched by the import of the Vedas’ (Garuda Purana).” (CC, Madhya 25.136–137)18

At this the pandits cried out: “He admits it himself: there is no commentary!”

Baladeva promised that in a few days he would show them the Gaudiyas' commentary on Vedanta. Amazed, the pandits suspected some ruse, but for the moment they said no more. And their demand carried weight in those days: a sampradaya was recognized as authoritative only if it had its own bhashyas on the “Vedanta-sutra,” the Upanishads, the “Vishnu-sahasra-nama” and the “Bhagavad-gita” — and the Rupanuga-sampradaya possessed no commentary on the “Vedanta-sutra”: in its place it revered the “Srimad-Bhagavatam,” which the Ramanandis did not accept. According to “Our Teachers,” Baladeva maintained that the Gaudiya Vaishnavas belong to the Madhva-sampradaya; but Madhvacharya said nothing of the worship of Sri Sri Radha-Govinda or of the raga-marga that Mahaprabhu taught — and the Ramanandis demanded that Mahaprabhu's teaching be grounded in a bhashya, or else the dispute would be decided in their favour.

The “Govinda-bhashya”

Eighteen days, it is said, were allowed him for a commentary on the sutras. How long he actually took to write it, the biographies tell differently: eighteen days, seven days, a few days, or three months.19

Deeply troubled, Baladeva went to Sri Govinda, Rupa's Deity, in His temple, bowed down before Him prostrating with eight limbs of the body, and told Him everything; he begged his guru and the Lord for the power such a work required. “Our Teachers” says that he first received the blessings of the Vaishnavas of the sampradaya and only then bowed before Govindadeva, asking for His mercy. According to one account, a garland slipped from Govindaji's neck, and the priests laid it upon Baladeva; he understood it as the Lord's token that he was now empowered for the task.

That same night Govinda appeared to him in a dream and said: “Compose the commentary. I Myself will approve it, and no one will find a flaw in it.” Baladeva himself, in the “Siddhanta-ratna,” which he also calls the “Bhashya-pithaka,” “the pedestal of the commentary,” writes that Sri Govinda-deva commanded him to compose this commentary — instructed and encouraged him in a dream (8.31). Full of joy and strength, he absorbed himself in meditation on Govinda's lotus feet and began to write.

The thought of such a commentary had lived in him before: while still studying Vedanta under Radha-Damodara and Pitambara, he had thought of an exposition of the sutras for Vaishnava students, and the debates with opponents in Galta only gave him the occasion to complete it. The commentary was finished within the appointed time. “By the Lord's blessing even the impossible becomes possible,” says one of the biographies: he expounded all five hundred of its sutras, kept within the time allowed, and missed none of the subtleties of the divine aesthetics of the pure Gaudiya Vaishnava path.

Baladeva dedicated the commentary to Govinda and named it after Him: since Govindaji Himself had commanded it to be written, it is the “Govinda-bhashya.” And all the glory he gave to Him as well. In the verse with which his work ends he says that the name “Vidyabhushana” and his renown were bestowed on him by Govinda Himself, who revealed this commentary in a dream:

“May Govinda be victorious, the friend of Radha, beautiful of form, who in a dream pointed out this commentary and, in His generosity, bestowed on me the ornament of learning and renown.”20

Govinda's Victory

The commentary won the king's praise. With it in hand Baladeva entered the debate again, silenced all the opponents' arguments and showed Gaudiya Vaishnava philosophy to be supreme. The scholars of other sampradayas, on seeing the commentary, were struck by its quality and were left speechless; the Gaudiya-sampradaya was hailed as the winner, to the great joy of the king and of every Gaudiya. Only a great acharya such as Shankara, Madhva or Ramanuja, says “Our Teachers,” could write a commentary on the “Vedanta-sutra” on his own — and the pandits were abashed. Relying on his commentary, Baladeva refuted the Ramanandis' arguments and established the supreme position of Sri Radha and Sri Krishna, showing that Their worship is the most perfect and pure form of religion; the good name of the Gaudiya school was preserved. But for him this was no worldly victory in debate; it was service to Rupa's Govinda: the Deity remained with His servants, and Mahaprabhu's teaching was defended.21

From that day the king of Jaipur ordered everyone to attend the arati of Sri Govinda, the Deity beloved of the Gaudiyas. So Mahaprabhu's teaching prevailed in Rajasthan, and to this day Sri Sri Radha-Govinda are worshipped in Jaipur. According to tradition, Baladeva also established the service of the Deity Vijaya Gopala in Galta.

The pandits, won over by his arguments, recognized him as an acharya and wished to become his disciples. Baladeva humbly declined. Of the four sampradayas, he said, the Sri-sampradaya is an authentic school, whose message is that serving God is the highest path; upholding the Gaudiya view, he meant it no disrespect, and to offend the Sri-sampradaya would be a grave offence. This is how a Vaishnava acts: he debated for the sake of truth, not to gain disciples, and the Sri-sampradaya remained for him a revered line of Vaishnavas.22

The Gaudiya world owes Baladeva much. He saved it from humiliation by its opponents, dispelled all doubts and won for the Gaudiyas recognition as a leading sampradaya. Had the principal Deity of the sampradaya, Rupa's Govinda-deva, passed under the control of another community, and had the Bengali priests been driven out of Amber, the Gaudiya-sampradaya in western India would have suffered a grievous blow. For the broad success of the Gaudiya mission had stirred up envy, and after the departure of Sri Jiva, until Vishvanatha and Baladeva came, the opponents took advantage of the fact that in Vraja it was hard to find an eminent Gaudiya able to answer them. “Our Teachers” says that thanks to Baladeva the Rupanuga-sampradaya was finally established as an independent tradition.

Victorious, Baladeva returned to Vrindavana, fell at Vishvanatha's lotus feet and told him everything. The Vaishnavas and residents of Vrindavana rejoiced, and Vishvanatha blessed him and congratulated both his disciples, Baladeva and Krishnadeva. He understood that he was leaving two experienced leaders who would continue the work of the community after his departure, and in his old age he was very happy.

Guardian of the Flame

On his return Baladeva began a commentary on the “Shat-sandarbha.” Soon afterwards Vishvanatha departed from this world, and it seemed to the Vaishnavas that a great lamp had gone out. Then they looked to Baladeva to tend that light — the foremost among those who understood Sri Chaitanya's teaching. After his teacher's disappearance he successfully led the Gaudiya Vaishnava movement from its centre in Vraja. One of the biographies remarks that Orissa's contribution to the success of this movement is no less than Bengal's, and that among the leaders from Orissa Baladeva is especially important — both as a leader at a turning point and as the author of a great many books.

He possessed an extraordinary mind and great strength of spirit: they sufficed not only to shield the sampradaya from the hostility of its rivals but to surpass them in thought. The age of Vishvanatha and Baladeva is the second notable period in the history of Gaudiya Vaishnava literature. Baladeva's life, says the same biography, was marked by two “great victories”: in the clash with a rival sampradaya, and in the Gaudiya exposition of Vedanta and the Upanishads — in commentaries and independent treatises. Both victories were service: the first preserved the seva of Govinda, the second showed the world that Mahaprabhu's teaching stands on the shruti. He was a writer of many-sided gifts, and in preaching as zealous as Sri Jiva.

Of his disciples the biographies name two as the most eminent, perfected souls: Sri Uddhava Dasa and Sri Nandana Mishra.23 Nandana Mishra, Baladeva's learned disciple, wrote a commentary on his “Siddhanta-darpana” and in its last verse named its author.

Through Uddhava Dasa a line runs from Baladeva to Jagannatha Dasa Babaji. Uddhava's disciple was Madhusudana Dasa — the celebrated Siddha Madhusudana Dasa Babaji of Surya-kunda — and he gave the dress of a babaji (paramahamsa-vesha) to Jagannatha Dasa Babaji.24

His Books: Philosophy

Baladeva wrote on philosophy, grammar, poetry and poetics (“Our Teachers” adds dramaturgy), and incidentally on history; some of his works are independent, others are commentaries on earlier books. The first and most famous of them is the “Govinda-bhashya,” a commentary on Vedanta in the light of the Gaudiya Vaishnava teaching of achintya-bhedabheda. As the last of the great expositors of Vedanta, Baladeva could survey all its currents and show the excellence and completeness of his own teaching. The “Govinda-bhashya” became the generally accepted Gaudiya commentary on Vedanta, and N. Sanyal's book on Mahaprabhu, published by the Gaudiya Math with a preface by Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, calls Sri Baladeva Vidyabhushana “the first Gaudiya commentator of the ‘Brahma-sutra.’”

The chief position Baladeva refutes in the “Govinda-bhashya” and his other philosophical works is the kevala-advaita of the Mayavadis: the doctrine of a Brahman without qualities, of the falsity of the world and of the jiva's having no real existence. His arguments not only defend theism but point to achintya-bhedabheda: the relation of Ishvara and the jivas, inconceivable to the human mind, is at once non-difference and difference. The shruti contains statements of both kinds; exclusive dvaita and exclusive advaita each take only their own passages, while Baladeva showed that every word of the shruti carries equal weight and gave a place to both in achintya-bhedabheda — without logical flaw. This is no bargain struck between two schools: so the shruti itself teaches, and so Mahaprabhu taught.25 His arguments are complete, clear and subtle, his works a notable contribution to Indian theistic thought, and through them the Gaudiyas came into living contact with other schools and took a prominent place in the religious life of India.

Why he undertook commentaries on the recognized shastras is explained by one of the biographies. Before Radha-Damodara and Baladeva, Gaudiya authors wrote independently and in a new way, but their works were valued only within the sampradaya; outside it they were not accepted as Vedanta and the Upanishads were. Baladeva therefore resolved to expound the principal recognized scriptures and make plain to all that Vedanta, the Upanishads and the ancient scholars support Gaudiya philosophy. Otherwise — for the religious mind of India is very conservative — the Gaudiyas would have been rejected as a dharma without support in Vedanta, and the treasures of the Gosvamis would have gone unappreciated.

On the “Govinda-bhashya” he also wrote a sub-commentary of his own, but later: at its beginning the “Siddhanta-ratna” is mentioned, which itself already refers to the “Govinda-bhashya” (8.31). The sub-commentary opens with obeisance to Sri Govinda, whom Rupa and Sanatana revealed, they “who dispelled the darkness of Mayavada”; then comes praise of Jiva: “May Jiva be my refuge, who delivered all the thinkers of the opposing schools — the Sankhyas, the Pashupatas, the vivarta-vadis”; then obeisance to Sri Chaitanya, Nityananda, Advaita and the other associates; then the history of the descent of the Gaudiya-sampradaya from Madhva and a list of acharyas from Madhva to Sri Chaitanya, beginning with Madhva's two direct disciples, Padmanabha and Narahari. This list was evidently taken from the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika,” Gopala-guru's “Sadhana-paddhati” and the writings of Dhyanachandra, Chaitanya Dasa and Manohara Dasa.26

At the very beginning Baladeva gives notice that the views and arguments of his commentary will follow the “Srimad-Bhagavata-purana,” approved by Sri Chaitanya, and the teaching of Madhva — “according to the view of Madhva Muni accepted by Sri Chaitanya.” One of the biographies concludes from this that the teaching of the Gaudiyas is at root the system of Madhva, polished by the teaching of the “Bhagavata” and given its own philosophical form by what Sri Chaitanya emphasized. A Gaudiya Vaishnava would put it more precisely: the Gaudiyas accept the succession from Madhva, but what Mahaprabhu “emphasized” — Radha-Govinda, the prema of Vraja, achintya-bhedabheda — is His own gift, not the polishing of another's system.27

The “Siddhanta-ratna,” or “Bhashya-pithaka,” is an independent work full of arguments that supports the nine principles established in the “Govinda-bhashya”: “May this golden pedestal, the ‘Siddhanta-ratna,’ be the foundation of the commentary on Vedanta that reveals Krishna and contains the nine truths” (8.32). It has eight chapters (padas); their subjects are the highest goal of the jiva (parama-purushartha), the greatness of Bhagavan, the supreme reality of Vishnu, His being known as the object of all the Vedas, the refutation of the impersonal Brahman and of the doctrine of “experience alone,” and finally the arguments that the highest goal is bhakti.28 It begins with obeisance to Shyamasundara, Sri Chaitanya, Vyasa, Rupa and Sanatana — the two who rose like two moons and dispelled the darkness of Mayavada; it ends with the glorification of Sri Govinda, and its closing verse says: “May the bee of my heart drink deep of the honey of prema from the flowers of truth brought by Sri Chaitanya and spread by Ananda-tirtha (Madhva).”29 Baladeva himself wrote a commentary on the “Siddhanta-ratna”; one of the biographies calls it the “Sukshma.” It is he, and not Rupa Gosvami, to whom they are sometimes ascribed, who actually wrote the “Siddhanta-ratna” and the “Kavya-kaustubha.”

The “Prameya-ratnavali” is a short and very important treatise on Gaudiya Vaishnava philosophy, set out in nine principles (prameyas). It begins with obeisance to the three principal Deities of the Gaudiyas — Govinda, Gopinatha and Madana-mohana — with a prayer for mercy to write of the nine most subtle truths; the second verse is obeisance to Sri Chaitanya with Nityananda and Advaita; in the next five he traces the Gaudiya-sampradaya from Madhva and lists the acharyas from Madhva to Sri Chaitanya. The nine principles are named in the verse sri-madhvah praha vishnum paratamam akhilamnaya-vedyam…, which says that Sri Madhvacharya taught them — and Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu taught the same principles:30

1. Vishnu is the highest truth.
2. He is known through the Vedas: He is their subject.
3. The world is real.
4. The jivas are distinct from Vishnu.
5. The jivas are servants of Vishnu.
6. Among souls there are grades: some are liberated, others bound.
7. Liberation is the attainment of Vishnu's lotus feet.
8. The way to it is unbroken bhakti.
9. The means of true knowledge are three: shruti, direct perception and inference.

Each truth then receives a chapter of its own. Baladeva unfolds them according to the Gaudiya teaching, citing the Upanishads (the Katha, Shvetashvatara, “Gopala-tapani,” Mundaka, Chhandogya and Isha), the “Bhagavata,” the “Vishnu-purana,” the “Narada-pancharatra,” the “Mahabharata,” the “Gita,” the “Harivamsha,” the “Gautamiya-tantra,” the smritis, the “Vedanta-sutra,” the Kauthumi-shakha of the Vedas and the “Brahma-samhita,” and with a verse of the “Padma-purana” (the very one the Ramanandis cited in Galta) he shows that one must follow one of the four recognized Vaishnava sampradayas. At the end he asks the learned to fix in their hearts these nine pearls of truth set forth by Madhva Ananda; and the last verse is an obeisance to Sri Chaitanya, by whose mercy the Gajapati Prataparudra was cleansed of all faults and found peace (this is the verse nityam nivasatu…, of which more below). The same verse opens the “Siddhanta-darpana.” Baladeva was evidently gladdened by the thought that Sri Chaitanya fully blessed Prataparudra, the ruler of his native Orissa.

The “Prameya-ratnavali,” together with the Sanskrit commentary “Kanti-mala,” was published by Gokula Gosvami and by the Calcutta Gaudiya Math; the author of the “Kanti-mala” called himself by the title “Vedanta-vagisha,” usual among pandits. Sanyal's book, published by the Gaudiya Math, says that these principles of Madhva were specially accepted by Shripada Baladeva in the “Prameya-ratnavali” — “which finally establishes the descent of the Sri Gaudiya-sampradaya, following Sri Krishna-Chaitanya, from the school of Madhva and justifies the name accepted among the devotees — Madhva-Gaudiya (or Brahma-Madhva-Gaudiya) sampradaya.” So Srila Bhaktisiddhanta calls it; and the same tradition of the Gaudiya Vaishnavas, from Kavi Karnapura to Baladeva, says that Sri Chaitanya received initiation in the line of the Brahma-sampradaya, through Ishvara Puri — hence the name “Brahma-Madhva-Gaudiya-sampradaya.” The same succession from Madhva as in the “Prameya-ratnavali” is given in the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” and by Gopala-guru.

The “Siddhanta-darpana” is a work on Vedanta with arguments in support of Gaudiya philosophy; Nandana Mishra, as has been said, wrote a commentary on it. Here Baladeva explains the nature of transcendental sound. The highest truth is one, but twofold — the Named and the Name:

“The highest truth is one, yet it appears in two ways — as the Named and the Name.”31

The Named is Krishna, the Name is the pranava, om. As the Named appears in many forms — Matsya, Kurma and others — so the Name appears as omkara, the gayatri, the Vedas. He is without beginning and without end, and therefore His glorification too is eternal; He comes into this world and leaves it by His own will. The book also speaks of the Lord's three potencies — of knowledge, of action and of power — of the jivas as His rays, His separated particles, and of the Vedas as spoken by the perfect Lord and untainted by the four defects, the Puranas and Itihasas being equal to the Vedas. A Bengali translation of the “Siddhanta-darpana” was published by Bhaktivinoda Thakura (1890).

One of the biographies also ascribes to Baladeva the “Vedanta-shyamantaka,” an exposition of the essentials of Vedanta, and quotes several of its thoughts: of all the means of knowledge (perception, inference, word, presumption, non-apprehension, probability, tradition) the best is the word of the shruti, for the Vedas are eternal, transcendental and untainted by the four defects (1.51); of all the forms of Lakshmi, Srimati Radharani is Lakshmi Herself, as Krishna is Bhagavan Himself among the avataras (2.37); the jiva is by nature a servant of Hari (3.11, after the “Padma-purana”). The closing verse says that this “Shyamantaka of Vedanta” was composed by a brahmana bearing the name Radha-Damodara and offered to Sri Radhika; the biography understands this as “at the behest of my gurudeva, the brahmana Sri Radha-Damodara.”32

The same biography sets out Baladeva's teaching as a whole. There are five tattvas — Ishvara, jiva, prakriti, kala and karma. Ishvara is omniscient, full of bliss and of all excellences; He is the Lord of Brahma and Shiva and remains when the world perishes. Krishna has three potencies — the higher (svarupa-shakti), the kshetrajna (jiva-shakti) and maya, as the “Vishnu-purana” teaches; God's body and His self are not different. Krishna is two-armed, holding the flute, in a form of eternity, knowledge and bliss; He is called Govinda and Gopala. Lakshmi is non-different from Him and accompanies each of His forms; when He appears in a human form she comes with Him, and Radha is the Supreme Lakshmi (the “Brihad-gautamiya-tantra”).33 Krishna is Bhagavan Himself (by Shaunaka's word in the “Bhagavatam”), and His worship is the highest. The jiva is an atomic particle of the spiritual potency, eternal and by nature a servant of Hari; surrendering to the guru, a devotee of Krishna, it attains by his mercy Krishna-bhakti, and with it Krishna Himself.

His Books: Commentaries

Baladeva expounded the ten principal Upanishads — the Isha, Kena, Katha, Prashna, Mundaka, Taittiriya, Aitareya, Chhandogya, Mandukya and Brihadaranyaka;34 the Gaudiya Math published his commentary on the “Ishopanishad” together with Madhva's commentary and the “Vedarka-didhiti” of Bhaktivinoda Thakura. He also wrote a commentary on the “Gopala-tapani Upanishad.”

His commentary on the “Bhagavad-gita,” the “Gita-bhushana-bhashya,” explains it continuously, verse by verse, in the light of achintya-bhedabheda; the title, as usual with him, is given at the end. The Gaudiya Math issued it three times, and Bhaktivinoda Thakura published the “Gita” with his own Bengali translation, the “Vidvad-ranjana-bhashya,” and Baladeva's Sanskrit commentary (1891). Srila B. R. Sridhar Maharaj, speaking of his own “Gita,” said that in our line the “Gita” was commented on by Srila Vishvanatha Chakravarti Thakura, Srila Baladeva Vidyabhushana and other teachers, and that Bhaktivinoda, in translating it into Bengali, relied on the commentaries of Baladeva and Vishvanatha (“Our Teachers”).

It is said that he also expounded the “Bhagavata”: one of the biographies calls his commentary on the Tenth Canto the “Vaishnava-nandini,” and Srila Sridhar Maharaj says that he commented both on the “Srimad-Bhagavatam” and on Jiva's “Shat-sandarbha.” The commentary on the “Shat-sandarbha” was published in Calcutta by Sri Shyamlal; another biography speaks of a commentary on the “Tattva-sandarbha.” At the beginning of the commentary on the “Tattva-sandarbha” Baladeva glorifies Jiva: “May Jiva Prabhu be our refuge, who with the nectar of speech restored the pure radiance of the Supreme Lord Krishna, dimmed by the mud of Sankhya, the dust of bad logic and the pit of vivarta.” There too he explains Jiva's words: “their” means Rupa and Sanatana, “friend” is Gopala Bhatta, and “the earlier Vaishnavas” are the books of Sri Madhva and others. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta refers to this commentary more than once in the “Anubhashya” (on CC, Madhya 6).

The commentary on Rupa's “Laghu-bhagavatamrita,” the “Saranga-rangada,” was published in Calcutta by Atul Krishna Gosvami in the 412th year of the Chaitanya era; the “Anubhashya” quotes it many times in explaining CC, Adi 5 — on the sixteen kalas, on Vishnu's being untouched by the gunas, on Shesha and other subjects. The commentary on the “Vishnu-sahasra-nama” is called the “Namartha-sudha”; Bhaktivinoda Thakura published the “Vishnu-sahasra-nama” with this commentary (1886), and the “Anubhashya” (on CC, Adi 3) cites from it the explanation of the names suvarna-varna, hemanga…. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta refers to Baladeva in other places of the “Anubhashya” as well — thus in CC, Adi 6 he cites the “Govinda-bhashya,” in Adi 13 the words of “Shripada Baladeva” on the Lord's appearance, and in Madhya 23 he advises studying the discussion of Sri Rupa and of “the commentator Sri Baladeva Vidyabhushana Prabhu” in the “Laghu-bhagavatamrita.”

Baladeva laboured especially over the books of Sri Rupa. His commentary on the “Stava-mala,” the “Stava-mala-vibhushana,” was written in 1686 Shaka (1764) and has been published by various editors. From it we know how the “Govinda-virudavali” came to be: Govinda gave His garland to a poet from the south. It also contains the closing verse of the commentary on the “eighteen metres” and the introduction to the “Govinda-virudavali” with quotations from the “Virudavali-lakshana”; there too Baladeva calls the “Gitavali” a work of Rupa — “forty-one gathas taught by Sri Rupa.”35 Srila Sridhar Maharaj recalls how in one of his commentaries Baladeva explains that Rupa and Sanatana showed the world Govinda, “who is always served by the Supreme Goddess of Fortune,” as one shows a jewel on the palm, turning it now one facet, now another (“Sri Guru and His Grace”).

He also wrote a commentary on Rupa's “Nataka-chandrika” (it has been published) and a commentary on Rasikananda's “Shyamananda-shataka.”

His Books: Grammar, Poetics, Poetry

Baladeva's grammar, the “Vyakarana-kaumudi,” has not been published and is almost lost; its manuscript was in Vrindavana with Radhacharana Vidyavagisha.

The “Aishvarya-kadambini” is a poem glorifying Krishna's deeds in Vrindavana and Gokula: 224 shlokas in seven “vrishtis” (chapters). Its subjects are Krishna's tripad-aishvarya and His appearance; the birth of Vasudeva, Nanda and others in the Vrishni line; the birth of Radhika; the festivities after Krishna's birth; His childhood and boyhood and the slaying of Kamsa; the hymns of the sages; the coming to Gokula and the pastimes there. The editor of the journal “Gaudiya” ascribed it to Vishvanatha Chakravarti, but the last verse of the manuscript names Baladeva Vidyabhushana as its author. According to other accounts, Vishvanatha had his own “Aishvarya-kadambini” — on dvaita and advaita, on achintya-bhedabheda — while Baladeva's is a book on Krishna's majesty without such discussion.36

The “Sahitya-kaumudi” is his commentary on Bharata's “Kavya-lakshana,” on which others had written before (the “Kavya-prakasha,” the “Kavya-pradipa”). At the end Baladeva says: “I have explained the whole ‘Kavya-lakshana’; this is a short commentary on the sutras of Bharata, composed by Vidyabhushana with the help of the existing commentaries of Mammata and others.” The manuscript scholar Peter Peterson mistakenly thought that the karikas on which the “Sahitya-kaumudi” is written belonged to Mammata. The treatise opens with a verse in glory of Sri Chaitanya:

“I worship Vishnu, the ocean of bliss, by whose mercy, when He dwells within us as Sri Chaitanya, all the sins of the Gajapati are washed away and he at once attains peace; no one can conquer Him, yet His saintly associates bring Him under their sway.”37

In the next verse Baladeva hints at the book's title. It has ten chapters and an additional one on rules not found in Bharata; in the ninth chapter he cites the figured verses (chitra-kavya) of Rupa's “Stava-mala.” The book was printed in the “Kavyamala” series.38 On the “Sahitya-kaumudi” he himself wrote a commentary, the “Krishnanandini”; its manuscript is kept in the collection of the Maharaja of Alwar.

He also had a commentary on Jayadeva's “Chandraloka” — apparently lost.

The “Chhanda-kaustubha” is an extensive treatise on prosody in 270 shlokas: the metres are described in stanzas glorifying Krishna. It begins with a well-known verse that Baladeva also places in other books of his: nityam nivasatu hridaye chaitanyatma murarir nah / niravadyo nirvritiman gajapatir anukampaya yasya — “May Murari, who is Chaitanya in essence, dwell eternally in our heart — He by whose mercy the Gajapati became faultless and found peace.”39 Raja Rajendralal Mitra mistakenly ascribed this work to Radha-Damodara; but at the end the author honours Radha-Damodara as “the ornament of the brahmana line, most dear to Hari,” so the writer is his disciple; and two manuscripts from Ayodhya name Vidyabhushana as the author outright. Krishnarama wrote a “Chhanda-kaustubha-tika” on the “Chhanda-kaustubha”; Baladeva himself also wrote a commentary on it.

The “Kavya-kaustubha” is a treatise on poetry; according to one of the biographies, an anthology of chosen Sanskrit verses for Vaishnavas. The “Pada-kaustubha,” according to another account, is a collection of select prayers.

The biographies also give full lists of his books — one of twenty-three titles, another with almost the same, adding the “Aishvarya-kadambini” and the commentary on the “Tattva-sandarbha”: the “Govinda-bhashya” and its commentary, the “Siddhanta-ratna” with the “Sukshma,” the “Vedanta-shyamantaka,” the “Prameya-ratnavali,” the “Siddhanta-darpana,” the “Sahitya-kaumudi” with the “Krishnanandini,” the “Kavya-kaustubha,” the “Vyakarana-kaumudi,” the “Pada-kaustubha,” the “Vaishnava-nandini,” commentaries on the “Gopala-tapani,” on the Isha and nine other Upanishads, the “Gita-bhushana,” the “Namartha-sudha,” the “Saranga-rangada,” the “Stava-mala-vibhushana,” and commentaries on the “Nataka-chandrika,” the “Chhanda-kaustubha,” the “Shyamananda-shataka” and the “Chandraloka.”

These books became a support for the acharyas who came after. Bhaktivinoda Thakura studied Baladeva's “Govinda-bhashya,” “Siddhanta-ratna” and “Prameya-ratnavali” in Puri, and later himself published many of his works.

Departure

How many years Baladeva lived is not known. His commentary on Sri Rupa's “Stava-mala” — more precisely, on the “Utkalika-vallari” included in it — is dated 1686 Shaka (1764); he was then perhaps about eighty-six, and this was evidently his last work. If he disappeared a few years after that, his life in this world lasted about ninety years. According to one of the biographies, Baladeva and his friend Krishnadeva Sarvabhauma departed from this world before the 1770s, and their places were taken by disciples of the next two generations, among them Vrindavana-chandra Chakravarti and Bankavihari Vidyabhushana.40 According to other accounts, the dated commentary on the “Stava-mala” shows that Baladeva was still alive after the battle of Plassey (1757), and he disappeared in 1768.41

The sources do not name the place of his departure. In the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math the day of his departure is Gaura-dashami of the month of Trivikrama, the same day as Ganga-dashahara and the appearance of Gangamata Gosvamini (in 2026, 24 June); his appearance day is not in the calendar, and the biographies give neither the one nor the other.

In Our Line

In the succession of true gurus of the Brahma-Madhva-Gaudiya-Sarasvata-sampradaya Baladeva is remembered constantly. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati sings in his parampara song: vishvanatha-bhakta-satha, baladeva, jagannatha, tanra priya bhaktivinoda — “Vishvanatha with his devotees, Baladeva, Jagannatha, his dear Bhaktivinoda”: homage to Vishvanatha and all his disciples, to Baladeva, to Baladeva's disciple Jagannatha and to his dear follower Bhaktivinoda. What makes a true guru is not a link of initiation in a hereditary chain but complete dedication to the highest truth (brahma-nishtha). Answering his opponents, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta spoke in accord with the teaching of the Gosvamis as carried on by Vishvanatha, Baladeva, Jagannatha Dasa and Gaurakishora Dasa Babaji.

In the chart of the Brahma-Madhva-Gaudiya-sampradaya given by Srila Sridhar Maharaj, Baladeva Vidyabhushana stands before Jagannatha Dasa Babaji. Asked about the gap of almost a century between them, Srila Sridhar Maharaj answered: our guru-parampara follows the ideal and not the body; it is a succession of instructing (shiksha) gurus. Baladeva's contribution, he says, is “no less important than that of the other great stalwarts in the line.” In a bodily sense he may have been a member of another line, the Madhva-sampradaya, but his contribution, especially his commentary on the “Vedanta-sutra,” which drew people to Gaudiya Vaishnavism, cannot be ignored, and our acharyas accepted it according to the degree, substance and purity of his thought. “We cannot dismiss him. He is our guru” (“Sri Guru and His Grace”).

The guru-parampara, Srila Sridhar Maharaj explains, is a current of spiritual truth and not a bodily succession: wherever by Krishna's will the highest is found, there it is accepted — from shastra-guru, shiksha-guru, diksha-guru, nama-guru. So too Baladeva's contribution has been accepted by our acharyas according to the substance and purity of his thought.

Our acharyas relied on him as a witness, too. Sanyal's book on Sri Krishna-Chaitanya, published by the Gaudiya Math, names among the later authors on whom it rests “Sri Baladeva Vidyabhushana, the first Gaudiya commentator of the ‘Brahma-sutra.’” “Our Teachers” compares Baladeva's contribution with that of Sri Jiva and calls his works a treasure offered at the lotus feet of Sri Rupa.

After the disappearance of Vishvanatha Chakravarti and Baladeva Vidyabhushana, according to one of the biographies, a fourth “dark age” began for Bengal Vaishnavism; “Our Teachers” adds that after Srila Baladeva's departure no acharya remained who was filled with his spirit of service, only some babajis absorbed in bhajana stayed true to the teaching, and pseudo-Vaishnava sects spread. But the Madhva-Gaudiya succession in the spirit of Rupa was not broken: teachers are sometimes solitary bhajananandis, sometimes preaching goshthyanandis, and the line that passed through Baladeva reached, through Jagannatha Dasa Babaji and Bhaktivinoda, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta.

  40. The printed text of this biography reads “before the seventh decade of the seventeenth century”; the sense is the eighteenth. It also says that he “attained nirvana” — not our word: a Vaishnava does not dissolve into the impersonal but leaves this world for the service of the Lord. The chronology is not consistent here either: Bankavihari, according to the same biography, finished his book in 1722, when Baladeva was in his prime. Bankavihari Vidyabhushana should not be confused with Baladeva.
  41. Thus the year of departure is: after 1764, at about ninety, “before the 1770s” — according to one biography; after 1757 — according to another; 1768 — according to a third.
